groups.title: Timing
groups.sub: When, and how it gets there

groups.title: Import and export
groups.sub: Bring it in, ship it out

topics.title: Your first animation
topics.intro: Draw a ball, give it a Position track, key it in two places and play it. That is the whole idea of SVGcinema, in six steps.
topics.goal: A ball rolls across the ground in two seconds, rests for a second at the end of the 3-second animation, and starts over: one track, two keyframes.

steps.title: Pick the Ellipse tool
steps.text: Press <kbd>O</kbd>. The Ellipse tool lives in the shapes button of the tools on the left: hold it to see the other shapes.

steps.title: Draw a ball
steps.text: Drag on the canvas, just above the ground. Hold <kbd>Shift</kbd> to keep it round. The new ball is selected, and the inspector on the right shows everything you can set on it.
steps.do: Drag on the canvas, above the ground. <kbd>Shift</kbd> keeps it round.

steps.title: Start a Position track
steps.text: Click {◆} beside Position in the inspector. Position gets its own row on the timeline, with a keyframe at the playhead, and the diamond turns amber.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 2s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler at the top of the timeline, to 2s. The inspector now shows the values at that moment.

steps.title: Move the ball
steps.text: Press <kbd>V</kbd> for the Select tool and drag the ball to the right, or type a bigger X in Position. A second keyframe lands at 2s: the editor fills in everything between the two.
steps.do: <kbd>V</kbd>, then drag the ball to the right.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The ball rolls across in two seconds, rests until the end of the animation (3 seconds in a new project), and starts over, as a new project loops forever. Next, give it a better feel in Easing.

topics.note: Every property in the inspector works the same way: start its track with {◆}, then change it at another time. A property without a track just changes, everywhere in time.
keys: Add a position keyframe at the playhead

topics.title: The editor at a glance
topics.intro: A quick look around the five areas you work in: the tools on the left, the canvas in the middle, the Layers panel, the inspector on the right and the timeline at the bottom. Each step asks for one small thing in one of them.

steps.title: Pick a tool
steps.text: The tools are in the narrow column on the left. Press <kbd>M</kbd> for the Rectangle tool: it lights up in the shapes button. A button with a small triangle holds more tools: press and hold it to see them.

steps.title: Draw on the canvas
steps.text: The canvas in the middle holds the artboard, your picture. Drag on it to draw a rectangle. A drawing tool stays on after each shape: press <kbd>V</kbd> or <kbd>Esc</kbd> to go back to Select.
steps.do: Drag on the canvas to draw a rectangle.

steps.title: Select in Layers
steps.text: The Layers panel lists every layer, the frontmost at the top; a padlock means it is locked. Click Sun to select it: it is selected on the canvas too.

steps.title: Change it in the inspector
steps.text: The inspector on the right shows everything about the selected layer. Type 170 in Position Y, in Transforms, and press Enter: the sun moves down, behind the hills.
steps.do: Type 170 in Position Y and press Enter.

steps.title: Scrub the timeline
steps.text: The timeline at the bottom shows what moves: the cloud already has a Position track. Drag the red playhead along the time ruler and the cloud drifts with it.
steps.do: Drag the playhead along the ruler.

steps.title: Export it
steps.text: On the right of the top bar are Undo, Redo, the keyboard shortcuts and Export. Click Export: the Export window previews the animation and makes it one animated .svg file (or an image, a video or a GIF).

topics.note: The ☰ menu at the top left has the file commands and everything else (Edit, Element, Animate, View, Help). F1 lists every keyboard shortcut.

topics.title: Projects, saving and files
topics.intro: SVGcinema keeps the project you are working on in this browser as you go: close the tab, and it is there when you come back. To keep a project for good, share it or work on several, save it as a .SVGcinema file.

steps.title: Open the main menu
steps.text: Click ☰ at the top left. The file commands are in it: New project, Open, Open recent, Save, Save as, Import files and Export.

steps.title: Save it as a file
steps.text: Click Save as…, name the file and click Save. A .SVGcinema file holds the whole project, images included. In Chrome and Edge you choose where it goes, and from then on Save (Ctrl S) overwrites it; other browsers download a new copy each time.

steps.title: Open a project
steps.text: Open… (Ctrl O) opens a .SVGcinema file, or an .svg file as a new project. Open recent lists the last projects you opened or saved here. With unsaved changes, you are asked to save them first.

steps.title: Start a new project
steps.text: Click New project…, set the canvas size and click Blank canvas. Open sample scene opens a tour of every feature instead.

topics.note: The browser keeps one project at a time, and clearing the site's data in the browser removes it: save the projects you want to keep. Beside the project's name, the top bar shows its file and whether it has unsaved changes.

topics.title: Select and transform
topics.intro: With the Select tool you pick layers and change them right on the canvas: drag to move, pull a handle to scale, turn the handle above to rotate. Every change shows in the inspector's numbers too.

steps.title: Select the box
steps.text: Click the box on the canvas. Handles appear around it, and the inspector on the right shows its properties.

steps.title: Move it
steps.text: Drag the box somewhere else. Hold <kbd>Shift</kbd> to move it straight across or straight up and down; the arrow keys nudge it by a pixel (10 with <kbd>Shift</kbd>).

steps.title: Scale it
steps.text: Drag the lower right corner handle with <kbd>Shift</kbd> held: the box grows and keeps its proportions, while the opposite corner stays put. <kbd>Alt</kbd> scales from the middle; the side handles stretch one way.

steps.title: Move the origin
steps.text: The small circle in the middle is the origin, the point the layer turns and scales around. Drag it to the lower left corner: it snaps to the corners and edges as it gets close.
steps.do: Drag the origin to the lower left corner.

steps.title: Rotate it
steps.text: Drag the round handle above the box: it turns around its origin, now the corner. <kbd>Shift</kbd> turns it in 15° steps.
steps.do: Drag the round handle above the box.

steps.title: Select both
steps.text: <kbd>Shift</kbd>-click the ball: one box goes around both, and dragging moves them together. Dragging across both, starting beside them, selects them too.

topics.note: Ctrl-click picks a layer inside a group. For exact values, type them in the inspector's Transforms section: Position, Scale, Skew, Rotate and Origin. Alt-drag a layer to drag a copy of it.

topics.title: Pen and pencil
topics.intro: The Pen draws exact paths, a point at a time: click for a corner, drag for a curve. The Pencil draws freehand and smooths the line for you.

steps.title: Pick the Pen
steps.text: Press <kbd>P</kbd>. The Pen lives in the pen button of the tools: hold it for the Pencil and the tools that add, remove and convert points.

steps.title: Click for corners
steps.text: Click on the canvas, then click again somewhere else: two corner points, joined by a straight line.

steps.title: Drag for a curve
steps.text: Press where the next point goes and drag: the point gets two handles, and the line bends toward them. <kbd>Alt</kbd> while dragging breaks the handle in two, <kbd>Shift</kbd> snaps it to 45° steps.
steps.do: Press and drag for a curved point.

steps.title: Close the shape
steps.text: Click once more, then click the first point: the path closes and gets a fill. To leave a path open, press <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Esc</kbd> instead: it gets a stroke.
steps.do: Click once more, then click the first point.

steps.title: Edit the points
steps.text: Press <kbd>A</kbd> for Edit path nodes and drag a point: the shape follows. Drag a handle to reshape a curve; double-click a point to switch it between smooth and corner.

steps.title: Draw with the Pencil
steps.text: Press <kbd>N</kbd> and drag a line: it is simplified and smoothed when you let go. End near where you started to close it into a shape.

topics.note: With the Pen on a selected path, click its outline to add a point, click a point to remove it, or click an open end to carry on drawing. While drawing, Backspace removes the last point.

topics.title: Shapes
topics.intro: Rectangles, ellipses, polygons, stars and lines share one button in the tools. Draw one, then set its corners, sides or points in the inspector.

steps.title: Draw a rectangle
steps.text: Press <kbd>M</kbd> for the Rectangle and drag on the canvas. <kbd>Shift</kbd> makes a square, <kbd>Alt</kbd> draws from the middle.
steps.do: Press <kbd>M</kbd>, then drag on the canvas.

steps.title: Round its corners
steps.text: In the Rectangle section of the inspector, type 24 in Radius or drag its slider. Its {◆} animates the radius.

steps.title: Pick the Star
steps.text: Press and hold the shapes button in the tools, then pick Star. Ellipse, Polygon and Line are there too.
steps.do: Hold the shapes button and pick Star.

steps.title: Draw a star
steps.text: Drag out from where its middle goes: the drag sets its size and angle. <kbd>Shift</kbd> keeps it upright, and <kbd>↑</kbd> <kbd>↓</kbd> while dragging add or remove points.
steps.do: Drag out from the star's middle.

steps.title: Set its points
steps.text: In the Star section, type 8 in Points or drag its slider. Ratio makes the points shorter or longer.

topics.note: A click without a drag places a shape at a standard size. A polygon or star keeps its settings until you edit its points by hand or give it Morph keyframes; then it becomes a plain path. Convert to path, in the shape's section, does that on purpose.

topics.title: Text and fonts
topics.intro: The Text tool puts editable text on the canvas. Type right there, then pick its font and size in the inspector: Google Fonts, basic system fonts, or fonts on your computer.

steps.title: Pick the Text tool
steps.text: Press <kbd>T</kbd>, or click the T in the tools.

steps.title: Click on the canvas
steps.text: Click where the text should start. A new text appears with its word selected, ready to type over. Drag instead to draw a box: the lines wrap to its width.

steps.title: Type your words
steps.text: Type: your words replace the selected one. Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> or click away to finish. Double-click a text to type in it again.

steps.title: Pick a font
steps.text: Click the Font field in Text appearance. Each font in the list shows your own text; type Pacifico in the search box and press Enter, or click a font.

steps.title: Set the size
steps.text: Type 72 in Size and press Enter. Style, bold and italic, letter spacing, alignment and case are in the same section.

topics.note: Convert to shapes, in the Text section, turns the letters into one path layer, which looks the same everywhere; it works with Google Fonts and fonts on your computer.

topics.title: Images and assets
topics.intro: Images wait in the Assets tab, beside Layers. Put one on the canvas as often as you like: the file is kept once in the project, and the export embeds it.

steps.title: Open Assets
steps.text: Click Assets above the Layers panel. Your images and SVG files are here; Add files brings in more, and so does dropping files on this tab.

steps.title: Place the picture
steps.text: Click the sunset: it goes in the middle of the canvas, as an image layer. Drag it to the canvas instead to drop it where you let go.

steps.title: Size it
steps.text: In the Image section of the inspector, type 240 in Size W and press Enter: the height follows, as an image keeps its proportions. Original size takes it back to its own pixels.
steps.do: Type 240 in Size W and press Enter.

steps.title: Move it into place
steps.text: Drag the picture into the frame. An image moves, scales, turns and fades like any other layer, and animates the same way.
steps.do: Drag the picture into the frame.

topics.note: Dropping image files on the canvas, or pasting an image, puts them straight on the canvas; so does Import files in the ☰ menu. PNG, JPG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, BMP, ICO, TIFF and HEIC work, and an SVG file comes in as layers you can edit.

topics.title: Booleans and align
topics.intro: Booleans combine two or more shapes into one new path: union, subtract, intersect or exclude. The align buttons beside them line layers up with each other, or a single layer with the canvas.

steps.title: Select both circles
steps.text: Drag a box on the canvas from an empty spot of the sky across both circles. Both are selected, and the bar at the top of the inspector offers the align and boolean buttons.
steps.do: Drag a box across both circles.

steps.title: Line them up
steps.text: Click Align vertical centers at the top of the inspector. With several layers selected they align to each other: the two circles now sit at the same height.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.text: Click Subtract, in the same bar. The upper shape is cut out of the bottom one: one new path called Subtract, with the moon's colour, in the moon's place.

steps.title: Centre it on the canvas
steps.text: Click Align horizontal centers. With one layer selected, it aligns to the canvas: the new moon moves to the middle.

topics.note: Union combines the shapes, Intersect keeps only their overlap, and Exclude keeps where they don't overlap. The shapes are combined as they look at the playhead, and undo brings the originals back. Distributing needs three layers or more. The right-click menu has the same commands, under Boolean and Align.

topics.title: Layers, groups and symbols
topics.intro: The Layers panel lists everything in the scene, the front layer at the top. Rename layers, change their order, group them, and hide or lock them to keep them out of the way.

steps.title: Rename a layer
steps.text: The snowman's head is selected, and it is still called Circle. Click its name at the top of the inspector, type Head and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>. Double-clicking a name in the Layers panel renames it too.
steps.do: Type Head in the name at the top of the inspector.

steps.title: Bring the scarf forward
steps.text: The scarf is behind the body. Click Scarf in the Layers panel, then Move layer up, the first button of the panel's top bar: the scarf moves above the body, in the list and on the canvas.

steps.title: Select the whole snowman
steps.text: Drag a box on the canvas from an empty spot of the sky across the snowman. It selects every layer it touches; the sky and the snow are locked, so they stay out of it.
steps.do: Drag a box across the snowman.

steps.title: Group them
steps.text: Click Group in the Layers panel's top bar, or press Ctrl G. The four layers go into one group, which moves, turns and fades as one.

steps.title: Lock the group
steps.text: Click the padlock on the group's row. A locked layer can't be picked or moved on the canvas; the eye beside the padlock hides a layer.
steps.do: Click the padlock on the group's row.

topics.note: Drag a row in the Layers panel to move it, or drop it into a group. A symbol is artwork whose copies share their contents: right-click a group and choose Make symbol (☰ › Element has it too), add copies from Assets › Symbols, and an edit to one reaches them all.

topics.title: Hyperlinks
topics.intro: Give a layer a link, and clicking it in the exported SVG opens a web page, an email, a phone number or an #anchor on the same page.

steps.title: Select the button
steps.text: Click Button in the Layers panel.

steps.title: Type the address
steps.text: In Hyperlink, the inspector's last section, type svgcinema.com in Link and press Enter. https:// is added for you, and the button's row in the Layers panel gets a link mark.

steps.title: Choose where it opens
steps.text: Once there is a link, Opens appears below it. Pick Same tab to open the page in place of yours; a new tab is the default.

topics.note: Links work in the exported SVG, not on the editor's canvas. A browser follows them when the SVG is part of the page (pasted in, or in an object tag, where Same tab opens the page inside the object's box), not when it is shown as an image. Web addresses, mailto:, tel: and #anchors only. Clear the field to remove the link; right-click › Hyperlink… edits the same link.

topics.title: Snapping, guides and rulers
topics.intro: Snapping lines things up as you move and draw: to other layers' edges and centres, to path nodes, to guides, to the grid and to whole pixels. Rulers and guides show where things are; the grid gives an even spacing.

steps.title: Show the rulers
steps.text: Click the grid button at the bottom right of the canvas, then Show rulers. Rulers appear along the top and the left of the canvas.
steps.do: Click the grid button, then Show rulers.

steps.title: Pull a guide
steps.text: Drag down from the top ruler onto the canvas and let go at 250: a tag shows where the guide is. Dropping a guide back on a ruler removes it.
steps.do: Drag down from the top ruler to 250.

steps.title: Snap the box to it
steps.text: Drag the box down towards the guide. Close to it, the box's bottom edge jumps onto the guide, and a magenta line shows the match. Hold <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> to move without snapping.
steps.do: Drag the box down to the guide.

steps.title: Show the grid
steps.text: Click the grid button again, then Front grid. The grid's size is at the bottom of the same menu.
steps.do: Click the grid button, then Front grid.

steps.title: Snap to the grid
steps.text: Click the magnet beside it, then Snap to grid. Moving and drawing now snap to the grid lines too; Enable snapping, in the same menu, turns all snapping off and on.
steps.do: Click the magnet, then Snap to grid.

topics.note: The guides are saved with the project; the rulers, grids and snapping settings are remembered in this browser. Keyframes in the timeline have their own switch, Snap keyframes, at the bottom of the magnet's menu.

topics.title: Fill and gradients
topics.intro: A shape's fill can be one colour, a linear or radial gradient, or nothing. The colour window edits them all, and while it edits a gradient you can drag the gradient's ends on the canvas.

steps.title: Select the beam
steps.text: Click the beam of light under the lamp. The inspector shows its Fill & stroke section.

steps.title: Open the colour window
steps.text: In Fill & stroke, click the swatch beside Fill. The colour window opens beside it: a colour area, hue and opacity sliders, and Hex and R G B A fields.

steps.title: Make it a gradient
steps.text: Click Linear gradient in the window's top row (None, Solid, Linear, Radial). The fill now fades from its colour to clear, and a bar of stops appears: click a stop to change its colour, or click the bar to add one.
steps.do: Click Linear gradient at the top of the window.

steps.title: Point it down
steps.text: While the window is open, the beam shows the gradient's two ends. Drag the hollow start to the top of the beam and the filled end to the bottom: the light now fades as it falls.
steps.do: Drag the hollow end to the top, the filled end to the bottom.

steps.title: Fade the fill alone
steps.text: Press Esc to close the window: all you changed in it is one undo step. Then type 70 in the Opacity row under Fill and press Enter. This opacity is the fill's own; the stroke has its own, and so does the whole layer, in Appearance.

topics.note: Fill and its Opacity each have their own {◆}. A gradient animates like a colour: its stops, angle, centre and radius blend, even from a solid colour. A CSS-only export animates only the stops' colours; the JavaScript export animates everything. A radial gradient shows a centre, a round handle for its size and direction, and a square one that makes it an ellipse.
keys: Pick the fill colour from the screen (in browsers with an eyedropper)

topics.title: Strokes and dashes
topics.intro: A stroke is the line along a path or a shape's edge: its colour, width, ends, corners and dash pattern. Animate the dash offset and the dashes travel along the line.

steps.title: Select the trail
steps.text: Click Trail in the Layers panel: a thin line is easier to pick there than on the canvas.

steps.title: Make it thicker
steps.text: In Fill & stroke, type 10 in Width and press Enter. The Stroke swatch above it opens the same colour window as Fill, gradients included.

steps.title: Round the ends
steps.text: In Appearance, under Stroke style, click the round Line ends button: the line now ends in half circles. The Line join buttons below it shape the corners the same way.

steps.title: Dash it
steps.text: Type 0, 22 in Dashes and press Enter: dashes of no length, 22 apart. With round ends, each of them is a dot.

steps.title: Start a Dash offset track
steps.text: Click {◆} beside Dash offset, under Dashes. Dash offset gets its own row on the timeline, with a keyframe at the playhead.

steps.title: Move the playhead to the end
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 3s, the end of the animation.

steps.title: Move the dashes
steps.text: Type -110 in Dash offset and press Enter, then press Space: the dots travel along the line. As 110 is five whole dash-and-gap lengths, they start over without a jump.

topics.note: On a closed shape, Align under Stroke style puts the stroke inside, on or outside the edge. Dashes have their own {◆} too, and patterns of different lengths blend. To draw a line on, animate Trim path's End from 0% to 100% instead.
keys: Add a dash offset keyframe at the playhead
Add a stroke width keyframe at the playhead
Add a stroke colour keyframe at the playhead
Add a trim end (draw on) keyframe at the playhead
Pick the stroke colour from the screen (in browsers with an eyedropper)

topics.title: Filters
topics.intro: Filters add effects to a layer: blurs, shadows and glows, colour changes and outlines. They stack in a list, and every setting of every filter can be animated.

steps.title: Select the moon
steps.text: Click the moon on the canvas, or its row in the Layers panel.

steps.title: Open the filter menu
steps.text: In the inspector's Filters section, click + Add filter…. The menu has three groups: Blur & shadow, Color and Edges.

steps.title: Pick Glow
steps.text: Click Glow. It appears as a card with its settings (X, Y, Blur, Spread, Color and Opacity), and the moon glows.

steps.title: Start a Spread track
steps.text: Click {◆} beside the glow's Spread. It gets its own row on the timeline, with a keyframe at the playhead.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 2s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 2s.

steps.title: Widen the glow
steps.text: Type 12 in Spread and press Enter. A second keyframe lands at 2s, and the glow grows into a wide halo.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The glow swells for two seconds, rests, and starts over. Filters animate in the JavaScript export; a CSS export keeps them still, as the note in Filters says.

topics.note: Filters apply from the top of the list down: drag a card by its head to reorder them, or use its arrows; the bin removes it. A card's chevron folds it to one row that sums it up, with a ◆ mark when something in it is animated.

topics.title: Masks and clipping
topics.intro: A mask shows the layers under it only where the mask is. Select the mask shape and what it should show, choose Create mask, and the top layer becomes the mask. It stays a layer you can move, edit and animate.

steps.title: Select the window and the view
steps.text: Drag a box on the canvas from the wall's top-left corner across the window. It selects every layer it touches: the window and the sea view behind it.
steps.do: Drag a box from the top-left corner across the window.

steps.title: Create the mask
steps.text: Click Create mask in the Layers panel's top bar, second from the right. The top layer, the window, goes into a Masks folder inside a new Mask group, and the view now shows only through it.
steps.do: Click Create mask in the Layers panel.

steps.title: Select the mask
steps.text: Click Window in the Layers panel, inside the Masks folder. A mask isn't drawn itself, but it is still a layer: its box shows where it is.

steps.title: Move it
steps.text: Drag inside the window's box on the canvas, to the right. The window moves over the view, which stays where it is: give the window's Position a track with {◆} and it pans across the view.
steps.do: Drag the window to the right.

topics.note: A mask works by opacity, so a soft or see-through mask shows its layers partly. Mask by, in the mask group's Group section, switches to Brightness: white shows, black hides. A clipping path (right-click › Create clipping path) uses only the mask's shape. Release mask, beside Create mask, puts the layers back.

topics.title: Appearance and blending
topics.intro: Appearance sets how a layer is drawn over what is behind it: its opacity and its blending, and for shapes the paint order and the stroke style. Opacity has its own {◆}, so a layer can fade in and out.
topics.goal: The blue light fades out of the mix in two seconds and comes back as the animation starts over: screen blending and two Opacity keyframes.

steps.title: Select the blue light
steps.text: Click Blue in the Layers panel.

steps.title: Blend it
steps.text: In Appearance, pick Screen in Blending. The red and green lights blend this way already: where the three overlap, their colours add up, to white in the middle.

steps.title: Start an Opacity track
steps.text: Click {◆} beside Opacity in Appearance. Opacity gets its own row on the timeline, with a keyframe at the playhead.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 2s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 2s.

steps.title: Fade it out
steps.text: Type 0 in Opacity and press Enter, or drag its slider all the way to the left. A keyframe lands at 2s, and the blue light is gone.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The blue light fades out over two seconds, stays out until the end of the 3-second animation, and comes back as it starts over.

topics.note: This Opacity is the whole layer's; the fill and the stroke have their own, in Fill & stroke. Isolate, beside Blending, keeps the layers inside a group blending with each other only, not with what is behind the group. Order paints a shape's stroke under its fill instead of over it.
keys: Add an opacity keyframe at the playhead

topics.title: Keyframes and tracks
topics.intro: Every property in the inspector can be animated. Start a track on it with {◆}, then change the value at another time: a keyframe lands under the playhead, and the editor fills in everything between.
topics.goal: The sun turns a quarter in two seconds, rests for a second, and starts over: two keyframes on one track.

steps.title: Select the sun
steps.text: Click the sun on the canvas, or its row in the Layers panel. The inspector shows everything you can set on it.
steps.do: Click the sun, or its row in Layers.

steps.title: Start a track
steps.text: Click {◆} beside Rotate. Rotate gets its own row on the timeline, with a keyframe at the playhead, and the diamond turns amber.

steps.title: Move the playhead
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 2s. The inspector now shows the values at that moment.

steps.title: Change the value
steps.text: Type 90 in Rotate and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>, or drag its label. A second keyframe appears at 2s, and the sun turns on the canvas.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The sun turns until 2s, rests until the end of the 3-second animation, and starts over. To change how it moves between two keys, see Easing.

topics.note: A property without a track just changes, everywhere in time. Once it has a track, every change adds or updates a keyframe at the playhead. To keep a track's keys but stop using them for a while, freeze it with the snowflake beside its name in the timeline.
keys: Add a position keyframe at the playhead
Add a rotate keyframe at the playhead
Add a scale keyframe at the playhead
Add an opacity keyframe at the playhead
Jump to the previous or next keyframe

topics.title: Shape morphing
topics.intro: A path's shape can be animated like any other property: its Morph track keeps the shape at each keyframe, and the editor blends the nodes between them. Morph into turns one shape into another in one go.
topics.goal: The blob grows points and flies into the star's place in a second and a half, holds there, and starts over.

steps.title: Select the blob
steps.text: Click the blob on the canvas, or its row in the Layers panel. The Morph section near the bottom of the inspector has what shapes can do: the node count, the Morph {◆}, Edit nodes and Morph into.
steps.do: Click the blob, or its row in Layers.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 1.5s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 1.5s. That is where the new shape will be.

steps.title: Morph into the star
steps.text: In the Morph section, open Morph into and pick Star. The blob gets a Morph track: its own shape at 0s, the star's at the playhead. The star layer is hidden, since the blob now becomes it.

steps.title: Click Edit nodes
steps.text: Click Edit nodes in the Morph section (it now reads Done editing). The blob's nodes show on the canvas, as they are at the playhead.

steps.title: Drag a node
steps.text: Drag the star's top point up. With a Morph track, moving a node changes the Morph keyframe at the playhead, or adds one when there is none there yet.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The blob grows its points on the way to the star, holds the new shape until the end of the 3-second animation, and starts over.

topics.note: Shapes morph best when they have about the same number of nodes, in the same order: the editor adds nodes where one has fewer. Rectangles and ellipses become plain paths when they start morphing. Add nodes (subdivide) gives a shape more nodes to bend.
keys: Add a morph keyframe at the playhead

topics.title: Motion paths
topics.intro: A motion path makes a layer travel along a line you drew. Set motion path turns the line into Position keyframes, one per node, timed so the layer moves at an even speed over the whole animation.
topics.goal: The paper plane flies along the dashed line over the 3-second animation, turning with each curve, and starts over.

steps.title: Select the plane
steps.text: Click the plane on the canvas, or its row in the Layers panel.
steps.do: Click the plane, or its row in Layers.

steps.title: Pick the path to follow
steps.text: In the inspector's Motion path section, open Follow (Set motion path…) and pick Flight path. The plane jumps to the start of the line, and its Position track gets a keyframe for every node of it.

steps.title: Turn it along the path
steps.text: Click the arrow button at the end of the Rotate row, under Transforms: Rotate along the motion path. The plane now points where it is going.
steps.do: Click Rotate along the motion path, beside Rotate.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The plane flies the whole line in 3 seconds, banking through the curves, and starts over.

topics.note: The plane's path is now its own: the dashed line is just another layer, so hide or delete it if it shouldn't show. Drag the path on the canvas to curve it, drag its handles to fine-tune, and double-click a segment to straighten it. Even speed along curves keeps the speed steady inside each curved segment too.
keys: Add a position keyframe at the playhead

topics.title: Trim path
topics.intro: Trim path shows only part of a stroke: from Start to End, in percent of its length, moved along it by Offset. Animate End from 0% to 100% and the line draws itself on.
topics.goal: The trail draws itself across the hills in two seconds, stays for a second, and starts over.

steps.title: Select the trail
steps.text: Click the yellow line, or its row in the Layers panel.
steps.do: Click the trail, or its row in Layers.

steps.title: Set End to 0
steps.text: In the inspector's Appearance section, under Trim path, type 0 in End and press Enter. The line disappears: none of it is shown.

steps.title: Start an End track
steps.text: Click {◆} beside End. End gets its own row on the timeline, Trim end, with a keyframe of 0% at the start.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 2s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 2s.

steps.title: Set End to 100
steps.text: Type 100 in End and press Enter. A second keyframe lands at 2s, and the whole line shows again.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The line draws itself on from its first node to its last.

topics.note: Animate Start the same way to erase the line from its beginning, or keep a short Start-to-End piece and animate Offset to send it along the path. The Strokes presets (Draw on, Erase, Travel…) write these keyframes for you.
keys: Add a trim end (draw on) keyframe at the playhead

topics.title: Animation presets
topics.intro: Presets are ready-made animations, in six groups: Entrances, Exits, Emphasis, Strokes, Color and Filters. A preset starts at the playhead and writes keyframes on the selected layers, only for the properties it animates.
topics.goal: The three balloons pop in one after another, then stay until the animation starts over.

steps.title: Select the balloons
steps.text: With the Select tool, drag a box around the three balloons on the canvas, starting on the empty sky. Every layer the box touches is selected.
steps.do: Drag a box around the three balloons.

steps.title: Open the presets
steps.text: Click Animate in the timeline's header, then Presets… at the top of its menu. The Presets window opens, on Entrances.

steps.title: Pick Pop in
steps.text: Click Pop in. Every tile plays its preset and names the tracks it writes (Scale · Opacity). The line beside Apply says when it runs and what it replaces; with several layers selected, Stagger starts each one 0.1s after the last.

steps.title: Apply it
steps.text: Click Apply (or double-click a tile). Each balloon gets Scale and Opacity keyframes: the first starts at the playhead, each next one 0.1s later. It is one undo step.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The balloons pop in, one after another, and stay until the 3-second animation starts over.

topics.note: Length, Stagger and Strength (how far it moves, grows or turns) change the preset before you apply it. Hovering a tile also shades its span on layers already in the timeline, and outlines in red the keyframes it would replace. A preset replaces only keyframes of its own properties inside its span, and ends (or starts) on the values the layer already has, so it slots into an animation you've made; one that runs past the end makes the animation longer. The Filters presets play in JS exports only.

topics.title: Editing many layers
topics.intro: Select several layers and change them as one: the inspector shows what they have in common, and every value, colour or keyframe you set goes on all of them. Select same picks every layer that shares a colour, a stroke or a type.
topics.goal: The three yellow stars turn together, then rest until the animation starts over; the white ones stay still.

steps.title: Select a yellow star
steps.text: Click the first star, or its row in the Layers panel.

steps.title: Select the same fill
steps.text: Click the Select same button beside the layer name at the top of the inspector, then Fill color. All three yellow stars are selected, and the inspector's header reads 3 layers.

steps.title: Start a track on all three
steps.text: Click {◆} beside Rotate. Each selected star gets its own Rotate track, with a keyframe at the playhead.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 2s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 2s.

steps.title: Turn them all
steps.text: Type 144 in Rotate and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>. Each star turns around its own centre, and gets its keyframe at 2s.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The yellow stars turn together; the white ones stay still.

topics.note: On the canvas, Shift+click adds a layer to the selection or takes it out; in the Layers panel, Ctrl+click does, and Shift+click selects a run of rows. A field whose value differs between the selected layers reads Mixed. On the canvas, one box goes around the whole selection: drag it to move them all, or its handles to scale and turn them together. To start layers one after another, use a preset's Stagger.
keys: Add a rotate keyframe at the playhead

topics.title: Build a rig: bones and attaching artwork
topics.intro: A rig is a chain of bones that carries your artwork: turn a bone and everything attached to it turns with it. Draw the bones over the artwork, chain them at the joints, then attach each part to its bone.

steps.title: Pick the Bone tool
steps.text: Press <kbd>B</kbd>. The Bone tool is in the bones button of the tools on the left: hold it to see the other bone tools.

steps.title: Draw the first bone
steps.text: Drag on the canvas from the shoulder to the elbow. A bone turns around its joint, where you started, and ends at its tip. It appears in the Layers panel as Bone 1.
steps.do: Drag from the shoulder to the elbow.

steps.title: Chain a second bone
steps.text: Start the next drag on the round tip of Bone 1, at the elbow, and drag to the wrist. A bone started on a tip is chained to it: Bone 2 hangs on Bone 1 and moves with it.
steps.do: Drag from the tip of Bone 1 to the wrist.

steps.title: Pick the Bind tool
steps.text: Hold the bones button in the tools on the left and pick Bind tool. It attaches layers to bones.
steps.do: Hold the bones button and pick Bind tool.

steps.title: Attach the upper arm
steps.text: Click the upper arm, then click Bone 1. In the Layers panel the upper arm moves into Bone 1; on the canvas it stays where it is.
steps.do: Click the upper arm, then Bone 1.

steps.title: Attach the forearm
steps.text: Click the forearm, then click Bone 2. Bone 2 hangs on Bone 1, so the forearm follows both.

steps.title: Try the rig
steps.text: Press <kbd>V</kbd> for the Select tool and drag Bone 2 around the elbow: the forearm turns with it. Drag Bone 1 and the whole arm turns at the shoulder.

topics.note: You can also attach a layer by dragging it onto a bone in the Layers panel, or with Attach to bone in the Rig section of its inspector. Each new bone starts with a Rotate keyframe at 0s, so turning a bone at another time animates it (see Pose and animate a rig). To change a bone's length or rest angle without animating it, use the Edit bone tool: attached artwork stays where it is.

topics.title: Pose and animate a rig: FK and IK
topics.intro: Pose a rig by dragging its bones. Drag a bone and it turns at its joint, carrying the bones below it (FK, forward kinematics); drag the tip at the end of a chain and the bones above it turn to reach the pointer (IK, inverse kinematics). Each pose is keyed on every bone of the rig.
topics.goal: The arm lifts at 1s, reaches up by 2.5s and starts over: two poses, each a keyframe on every bone.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 1s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 1s. The first pose goes there.

steps.title: Turn the upper arm (FK)
steps.text: With the Select tool, drag Bone 1 up around the shoulder. It turns at its joint and everything below it follows: that's FK. Every bone of the rig gets a keyframe at 1s.
steps.do: Drag Bone 1 up around the shoulder.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 2s
steps.text: Drag the playhead on to 2s, for the next pose.

steps.title: Reach up with the hand (IK)
steps.text: Drag the round tip of Bone 2, at the wrist, upwards. Both bones turn so that the tip follows the pointer: that's IK. <kbd>Alt</kbd>+drag on a bone does the same.
steps.do: Drag the tip of Bone 2 upwards.

steps.title: Retime a pose
steps.text: In the timeline, Bone 1 has a Pose row with a diamond at each pose. Drag the one at 2s to 2.5s: the keyframes of every bone at that time move with it.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The arm lifts, reaches up, holds until the end of the 3-second animation and starts over.

topics.note: Key whole rig, in the Bone section of the rig's top bone, is what keys every bone at once; turn it off to key only the bone you drag, for overlapping action. Click a Pose diamond to select all its keyframes, then press Delete to remove the pose.
keys: Jump to the previous or next keyframe

topics.title: Limits and IK stops
topics.intro: A limit keeps a bone's turn inside a range, so an elbow or a knee only bends the way it should. An IK stop ends a chain at a bone: dragging a tip below it turns only the bones from there down.

steps.title: Select the forearm's bone
steps.text: With the Select tool, click Bone 2, the bone along the forearm. The inspector shows its Bone section.

steps.title: Turn on Limit rotation
steps.text: In the Bone section, tick Limit rotation. A Range row appears with a min and a max, −90° and 90° to start with: how far the bone may turn either way from the angle it was drawn at.

steps.title: Let the elbow bend one way
steps.text: Type 0 in max and press Enter. Bone 2 can now bend the elbow further, up to 90°, but never open it wider than it was drawn.

steps.title: Reach down with the hand
steps.text: Drag the round tip of Bone 3, at the hand, down and to the right. The elbow stays bent and the shoulder turns instead: IK keeps every bone inside its limits.
steps.do: Drag the tip of Bone 3 down and to the right.

steps.title: Make Bone 2 an IK stop
steps.text: Click Bone 2 again, then tick Pin: IK stops at this bone. Its joint turns square: a chain dragged from below now starts there.
steps.do: Click Bone 2, tick Pin: IK stops at this bone.

steps.title: Drag the hand again
steps.text: Drag the tip of Bone 3 up. Only Bone 2 and Bone 3 turn: the upper arm stays where it is.
steps.do: Drag the tip of Bone 3 up.

topics.note: Limits apply while you drag bones, with FK and with IK; a value you type in Rotate isn't limited. An IK stop changes only IK: the pinned bone still turns with the chain below it, and dragging the bones above it works as before.

topics.title: Pins and mesh warp
topics.intro: Pins bend artwork without bones. Put pins on a shape and drag one: the artwork bends, held by the pins that stay put. A path bends through its own nodes; an image, a text or a group bends through a mesh of triangles laid over it.
topics.goal: The flag's free end swings down in 1.5 seconds, bending the whole flag, then holds and starts over.

steps.title: Pick the Pin tool
steps.text: Press <kbd>W</kbd>. The Pin tool is in the pins button of the tools on the left.

steps.title: Pin the flag by the pole
steps.text: Click the flag close to the pole. A pin appears where you clicked, and a mesh of triangles covers the flag: it's a group, so it bends through the mesh.
steps.do: Click the flag close to the pole.

steps.title: Pin its free end
steps.text: Click near the other end of the flag for a second pin. A pin you don't move holds the artwork where it is.
steps.do: Click near the flag's other end.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 1.5s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 1.5s.

steps.title: Bend the flag
steps.text: Drag the second pin down. The flag bends between the two pins, and the pin gets its own track, Pin 2: at rest at 0s, bent at 1.5s.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The flag bends until 1.5s, holds until the end of the 3-second animation and starts over.

topics.note: Drag the ring around the selected pin to turn it, and Alt+drag a pin to move it without bending. The Pins section of the inspector edits the selected pin: Reach sets how far the pins pull, Mesh how fine the triangles are, and Remove pin takes it off. Rectangles and ellipses become paths when they get their first pin.

topics.title: Pins that follow bones
topics.intro: A pin can follow a bone instead of keyframes of its own: it sits at the bone's joint and moves and turns with it, so the rig bends the artwork. It suits things that bend along their length, like a tail, a sleeve or this worm.
topics.goal: The worm wiggles with its three bones: its pins follow them, without a keyframe of their own.

steps.title: Select the worm
steps.text: With the Select tool, click the worm beside the bones lying along it. The bones already wiggle, but they don't carry the worm.
steps.do: Click the worm beside its bones.

steps.title: Pick the Pin tool
steps.text: Press <kbd>W</kbd>. The bones stay on the canvas while the Pin tool is on.

steps.title: Turn on Bind to bones
steps.text: Click Bind to bones in the bar above the canvas. It is there while a layer that takes pins is selected and the scene has bones.
steps.do: Click Bind to bones above the canvas.

steps.title: Click each bone
steps.text: Click Bone 1, Bone 2 and Bone 3. Each click adds a red pin at that bone's joint, bound to it; clicking a bound bone again unbinds it. Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> when you're done.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The bones wiggle and the worm bends with them: in the Pins section, each pin names its bone instead of a Position.

topics.note: Bound pins work together with ordinary ones on the same layer: add a few more to hold a part still, or to bend it by hand. The Bind tool binds a pin you already have: click the pin, then the bone. A bone inside a pinned group can't take the group's pins, since it already moves the artwork.

topics.title: The timeline
topics.intro: The timeline shows time from left to right: the ruler and the red playhead on top, then a row for each animated layer with a row for each of its tracks and their keyframes. A new project is 3 seconds long and loops forever.
topics.goal: The bird sets off at half a second and crosses the sky as the cloud drifts by, then the 3-second animation starts over.

steps.title: Scrub through it
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler. The canvas shows every moment as you go, and the time in the timeline's header follows.

steps.title: Zoom the timeline
steps.text: Drag the zoom slider at the right of the timeline's header to the right, or hold <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> and scroll over the timeline. The seconds spread out, so keyframes are easier to pick; scroll sideways for the rest.
steps.do: Drag the zoom slider to the right.

steps.title: Box-select keyframes
steps.text: On the bird's Position row, drag a box from the empty space after its last keyframe, left past its first one. Both keyframes are selected. A click selects one keyframe, and <kbd>Shift</kbd>+click adds one or takes it out.
steps.do: Drag a box around the bird's two Position keyframes.

steps.title: Drag them later
steps.text: Drag one of the selected keyframes half a second to the right: they all move together, and the bird now sets off at 0.5s. A tip shows the time as you drag; keyframes snap to the playhead, to other keyframes and to 0.05s steps.
steps.do: Drag the first keyframe 0.5s to the right.

steps.title: Turn off Loop preview
steps.text: Click the loop button, right of play. With it off, the preview plays once and stops at the end. It changes only the preview: the animation still loops forever when exported.
steps.do: Click the loop button, right of play.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The animation plays once, to the end of its 3 seconds, and stops. <kbd>Home</kbd> takes you back to the start.

topics.note: The white line after the last second marks the end of the animation: drag it, or click the length after the time in the header, to make the animation longer or shorter. Repeat and Direction are in the inspector when nothing is selected. Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V copy the selected keyframes and paste them at the playhead; right-click a keyframe for more.
keys: Jump to the previous or next keyframe
Move the selected keyframes one frame (Shift: 10)

topics.title: Easing
topics.intro: Easing is how a property gets from one keyframe to the next: at an even speed, speeding up, slowing down, overshooting or bouncing. Each keyframe has its own, for the way to the next key.
topics.goal: The ball drops and bounces to a stop, then starts over: the same two keyframes, with Bounce out.

steps.title: Play it as it is
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The ball falls at one even speed and stops dead: its keyframe is set to Linear.
steps.do: Press <kbd>Space</kbd> and watch the ball fall.

steps.title: Pick the way between the keys
steps.text: In the timeline, click the line between the ball's two keyframes. That selects the first key: its easing is the way to the next one.
steps.do: Click the line between the two keyframes.

steps.title: Open the Easing panel
steps.text: Click the curve button in the timeline's header, left of Animate. The Easing panel opens above the timeline.

steps.title: Pick Out, then Bounce
steps.text: Click Out at the top of the panel, then Bounce. The curve shows the new timing: the ball now lands and bounces.

steps.title: Play it again
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. Same two keys, a different feel. Drag the curve's two handles for a timing of your own, and save it as a preset.

topics.note: In, Out and In-Out decide where the change happens: In starts slowly, Out ends slowly, In-Out does both. Hold keeps the value until the next key, then jumps.
keys: Jump to the previous or next keyframe

topics.title: Graph editor
topics.intro: The graph editor opens one track into a curve of its value over time. Drag a key to change its time and value, and drag the handles between two keys to shape the easing yourself.
topics.goal: The sails turn a quarter turn over the whole 3 seconds, at a steadier pace, so the loop never stops.

steps.title: Select the sails
steps.text: Click the sails on the canvas, or their row in the Layers panel. They have a Rotate track: a quarter turn in 2 seconds, slow at both ends.
steps.do: Click the sails, or their row in Layers.

steps.title: Turn on Graph
steps.text: Click Graph at the right of the timeline's header. The Rotate track opens into a curve, with its value at the playhead beside it.

steps.title: Drag a key
steps.text: Drag the key at 2s to the right, to 3s. A readout shows the time and value as you drag; up or down changes the value (<kbd>Shift</kbd> keeps the drag to one direction). Now the turn lasts the whole animation.

steps.title: Shape the curve
steps.text: Drag the round handle on the left up, toward the middle of the curve. The turn now starts faster: the curve is an easing of your own.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The sails speed up and slow down as the curve says. Four sails look the same after a quarter turn, so the loop is seamless.

topics.note: The graph shows one number track at a time: the selected keyframe's, or else the selected layer's first one; click another track's name to graph that one. Points such as Position and Scale show X and Y as two curves. Colours, gradients, dash patterns and morphs have no graph.
keys: Jump to the previous or next keyframe

topics.title: Onion skin
topics.intro: Onion skin draws faint copies of the selected layers a few moments before (blue) and after (red) the playhead, so you can see where they come from and where they go. The copies are only on the canvas: they are never exported.

steps.title: Select the ball
steps.text: Click the ball on the canvas, or its row in the Layers panel. Onion skin shows the selected layers only.
steps.do: Click the ball, or its row in Layers.

steps.title: Turn on Onion skin
steps.text: Click Onion skin at the right of the timeline's header. Faint copies of the ball appear ahead of it in red: where it will be in the next three tenths of a second. At 0s there is nothing before it.

steps.title: Move the playhead to 1s
steps.text: Drag the red playhead along the time ruler to 1s, the top of the hop. The copies follow: blue ones where the ball was, red ones where it is going. Their spacing shows the speed.

steps.title: Space them out
steps.text: Click the arrow beside Onion skin for its settings, and type 0.2 in Every. Before and After set how many copies (up to 10), Fade how strong the nearest ones are.
steps.do: Click the arrow, then type 0.2 in Every.

steps.title: Play it
steps.text: Press <kbd>Space</kbd>. The copies hide while it plays, and come back when you pause.

topics.note: Onion skin is also in View › Onion skin. Whether it is on, and its settings, are remembered in this browser, for every project.

topics.title: When it starts: load, hover, click, scroll
Connect your own API key
topics.intro: The design agent chats in the Agent panel with a model from a service you have an account with: OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq or any OpenAI-compatible service. You connect it once with your own API key, and its requests use your own credit with that service.

steps.title: Open the Agent panel
steps.text: Click Agent in the top bar, or press Alt A. The panel docks on the right of the editor.

steps.title: Choose your own API key
steps.text: The first time, the panel asks how you want to connect. Pick Your own API key and click Continue. You can switch later, under How you connect in the agent's settings.

steps.title: Pick the provider
steps.text: Pick the service your key is from. OpenRouter is recommended: one key for chat and images, with many models. Custom takes any OpenAI-compatible address and a model name. Click Continue: the agent's settings open.

steps.title: Make a key on the provider's website
steps.text: Sign in on the provider's website, create an API key and copy it. The website also shows its prices and what you have used: the agent's requests use the credit of that account.
steps.do: Create an API key on the provider's website and copy it.

steps.title: Paste the key
steps.text: Paste it in API key, under Agent model; the eye button beside it shows it. The key is kept in this browser only and sent straight to the provider: SVGcinema never sees it.

steps.title: Pick a model and test it
steps.text: Pick a model in Model (Other model… takes any name the provider uses), then click Test. It checks that the service can be reached from this page, knows the model and can use tools, and whether the model can see images.

steps.title: Back to the chat
steps.text: Click ‹ at the top of the panel. Describe what to make and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>: the agent works in this project, and each request is one undo step. The model's name under the message box switches to another of the provider's models.
steps.do: Click ‹ to go back to the chat.

topics.note: Keys are kept in this browser, one per provider, never in a project file. Remove keys, under Privacy in the agent's settings, clears them; so does clearing the site's data in the browser.

topics.title: Use your AI assistant
topics.intro: No API key needed: an AI assistant you already use in your browser, such as Claude in Chrome, can edit the open project with SVGcinema's own editing tools, on its own subscription. You chat with it in its own window; the Agent panel shows what it does.

steps.title: Open the Agent panel
steps.text: Click Agent in the top bar, or press Alt A. The panel docks on the right of the editor.

steps.title: Choose your AI assistant
steps.text: The first time, the panel asks how you want to connect: Your AI assistant is picked first. Click Continue: the panel lists how to connect, step by step.

steps.title: Copy the starting message
steps.text: Click Copy under Start with this message. It asks your assistant to run window.svgcinema.help(), SVGcinema's guide to its tools, and follow it. Using Claude? Download the skill once instead, add it in Claude's settings under Skills, and just ask.

steps.title: Paste it in your assistant
steps.text: Open your assistant in the SVGcinema tab, paste the message in its chat and add what to make. It must be able to run scripts on web pages: allow it on this site if it asks.
steps.do: Paste the message in your assistant's chat and say what to make.

steps.title: Watch it work
steps.text: Its steps show in the panel as it works, with Stop. Editing is paused meanwhile, so everything it does for one request is one undo step. Before it deletes layers, the panel asks you.
steps.do: Watch its steps in the Agent panel.

steps.title: Undo, or ask for more
steps.text: Under its steps, Undo takes back everything it did, in one step. Ask for changes in your assistant's own window: each request shows here as a new set of steps.
steps.do: Click Undo to take it all back.

topics.note: Pictures follow Images on the connect screen: your assistant's own (when it can't hand one over, the panel asks you to drop it in), the image model of your API key settings, or vector shapes only. Let assistants edit this project turns it all off. Other assistants can read the plain-text guide (the guide for AI assistants, on the connect screen); SVGcinema's llms.txt file points them to it.

topics.title: Pictures and vector
topics.intro: The design agent can make pictures with an image model and put them on the canvas, or draw artwork as vector layers whose parts can move on their own. You set it up under Images in the agent's settings; pictures use your own credit with the image service.

steps.title: Open the agent's settings
steps.text: Open the Agent panel (Agent in the top bar) and click the cog at its top. The agent needs to be connected with an API key first: see Connect your own API key.

steps.title: Pick an image model
steps.text: Under Images, Provider is the service that makes the pictures: the agent's own when it makes them (OpenRouter, OpenAI or Gemini), or another one with a key of its own. Pick a model in Image. With None, the agent draws everything as vector shapes.

steps.title: Test it
steps.text: Click Test under the model: it makes one small test image, which uses a little of your credit. With Transparent background on, it checks that too: when a model can't make one, SVGcinema asks for a flat green background and removes it.

steps.title: Ask for a picture
steps.text: Back in the chat (‹), ask for a picture. Before making one, the agent shows a card with the prompt (you can edit it), the model, the size, the background and about what it costs, when the price is known.
steps.do: Ask for a picture in the chat.

steps.title: Generate it
steps.text: Click Generate, or Cancel. The picture goes into the project's Assets and the agent puts it on the canvas: one layer, which moves as one piece. Don't ask again skips the card; Ask first in Settings brings it back.

steps.title: Vector for parts that move
steps.text: With Prefer vector when parts move on, under Images, the agent makes artwork whose parts move on their own as vector: separate, editable layers. Vector says who draws it: the agent itself, or a vector model (on OpenRouter or a Custom service).
steps.do: Ask for artwork whose parts move.

topics.note: OpenRouter's list of image models is read live, so new ones appear by themselves, and the menus show about what one image costs when OpenRouter's price list has it. What you may do with generated images is set by the image service's terms.
